options.text: The friction of air particles on the body creates drag.
The higher the velocity through the air, the more aerodynamic force is generated.
The air becomes noticeably more solid and its force acts on the shape/surface presented to it.

A hollow hemisphere (round reserve canopy) has more drag.
A RAM-air canopy shape converts the airflow into lift by creating a pressure differential between the top and bottomskins.

questions.stem: What is an advantage of a RAM-air canopy?

options.text: It can be controlled and slowed down for landing.
Because it can be slowed down, a parachute landing fall will never be necessary again.
Malfunctions on opening are completely eliminated.
The RAM-air canopy automatically turns into the wind for landing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What is an advantage of a RAM-air canopy?

options.text: It glides forwards when sinking, thus allowing longer distances to be covered in flight.
One can achieve forward ground speed when flying into the wind, provided that the wind is not stronger than the forward speed designed into the RAM-air canopy.
One can fly crosswind with a RAM-air canopy resulting a crabbing sideways to the wind direction.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What are the stabilizers on the sides of RAM-air canopy for?

options.text: They stabilize the canopy when going straight ahead, like a daggerboard on the hull of a sailing ship.
They reduce the pressure equalization between the airflows over and under the canopy at the outer cells and thus stabilize the wing aerodynamically.
They keep the construction of the canopy stable at the outer cells, where the greatest force prevails.
They stabilize the slider at the opening.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Where does the airflow at the RAM-air canopy create its greatest lift effect?

options.text: at the rear third of the bottom skin.
on the topskin, just before the airflow break-away edge.
on the front third of the topskin

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: During its flight through the air, the RAM-air canopy generates not only lift, but also drag which reduces the overall flight performance. What resistance forces are these?

options.text: Surface and shape drag of the canopy.
Induced drag (wake vortex) and interference drag (superposition of individual resistances)
residual drag (pilot chute, deployment bag, lines, slider, risers, parachutist, parachutist clothing).

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Because air always seeks the least resistance or equalize pressure, the airflow over the middle cell is highest and at the outer cells lowest, with a tendency towards zero. Which statement is therefore correct?

options.text: The dynamic pressure is highest in the centre cell and lowest in the outer cells.
When slowing down, lift is first lost at the centre cell.
The steering lines must be attached across the entire width of the canopy.
This is why zero porosity fabric for a canopy is better than F-111 fabric.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: With a RAM-air canopy lift is most favourable when flying straight ahead, because

options.text: the total aerodynamic force of the canopy counteracts gravity exactly.
the weight of the parachutist is not influenced by any additional force (e.g. centrifugal force).
the flow around the canopy is laminar.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: In practice, we distinguish between slow- and high-speed flight profiles. What are the characteristics of a high-speed profile?

options.text: High canopy depth, low aspect ratio, short lines, high canopy thickness
High aspect ratio, shallow canopy depth, steep line trim, shallow canopy thickness
Thin lines, zero-porosity fabric, collapsible sliders.
Small aspect ratio, shallow canopy depth, microlines, shallow canopy thickness

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: In practice, we distinguish between slow and high-speed flight profiles. What are the characteristics of a slow flight profile?

options.text: High canopy depth, low aspect ratio, flat line trim, high canopy thickness
High aspect ratio, shallow canopy depth, steep line trim, shallow canopy thickness
Thin lines, F-111 fabric, collapsible slider.
low aspect ratio, shallow canopy depth, microlines, shallow canopy thickness

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What is the difference between a high-speed and a slow-speed profile of a RAM-air canopy?

options.text: a slim, slightly domed shape with low drag.
a thick, uniform shape with the greatest thickness in the first third of the wing.
less total surface area to avoid resistance and by stabilizers.
a larger canopy and shorter lines.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: When slowing down the RAM-air canopy the angle of attack is increased by changing the chord line in relation to the airflow. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The RAM-air canopy is slowed down by pulling the steering lines in parallel. This effect (flare) can be used for landing.
The slowing down effect only lasts as long as the RAM-air canopy is still moving and there is airflow. When the RAM-air canopy comes to a standstill, it goes into deep stall.
If the RAM-air canopy is over-braked, a stall is created.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What is the difference between angle of attack and angle of incidence?

options.text: The angle of attack is changed by the parachutist by pulling the steering lines, while the angle of incidence is specified by the manufacturer but can be changed by riser control.
Angle of attack relates to a canopy in flight, angle of incidence relates to a canopy on landing.
As the angle of attack is reduced, the angle of incidence is increased.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: The lift-increasing effect of the slowed down RAM-air canopy is based amongst other things on the

options.text: increase in the rate of descent
Increase of the angle of attack.
reduction of the angle of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What happens in a stall?

options.text: The airflow on the topskin no longer follows the wing shape and separates from the trailing edge.
The wake vortex deforms the canopy.
The wing undercuts the airflow and may fold down from the front edge.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: One speaks of a stall of the airflow in a RAM-air canopy, when

options.text: the airflow separates from the topskin of the canopy.
the airflow around the wing is so slow that buoyancy can no longer carry the parachutist.
there is no pressure differential between top and bottom skin anymore.
the stagnation point moves to the back.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How do the aerodynamic conditions of a RAM-air canopy change when approaching the stall of the canopy?

options.text: The pressure differential remains constant even in the vicinity of the critical angle of attack (approx. 2/3 low and 1/3 high pressure).
The airflow speed is reduced on the topskin.
Airflow is no longer able to follow the upper wing curvature; the boundary layer separates.
Air flow stops along the bottom of the canopy profile.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: On which parameters does the stall point essentially depend?

options.text: ratio of the weight of the parachutist to the size of the canopy, altitude and speed.
ratio of the weight of the parachutist the size of the canopy and the brake position.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which flight behaviour corresponds to a stall?

options.text: Smooth, trimmed glide at full speed.
The opening phase in which the slider is still at the base of the bottom skin.
The canopy collapses due to overbraking and then begins to lose its load capacity very quickly.
The abrupt pulling down of a steering line from full flight, followed by several line twists due to the parachutist's inertia in relation to the canopy.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How do you flare your canopy to land?

options.text: By pulling both steering lines simultaneously to the 100% brake position. Keep hands parallel to the horizon and keep the canopy under control.
Pull the steering lines down in a controlled and progressive manner. In order to estimate the height and correct timing, look down and ahead at approximately 45°.
I flare faster or slower corresponding to the speed at which the ground approaches.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Is it possible that a canopy flies backwards in relation to the ground when braking?

options.text: Yes, when flying against the wind a backwards drift may occur depending on the wind speed.
Yes, this always happens when you overbrake the canopy.
This possibility can only occur if I brake with the front risers.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: A turn can be flown with a RAM-air canopy using the steering lines, the rear or front risers as well as by shifting weight. What are the flight mechanics of such turns?

options.text: Nothing, since the total mass does not change, all parameters remain constant.
The canopy tilts in the turn. It is therefore relevant whether the turn is with the wind or into the wind.
The resulting centrifugal force increases the weight of the parachutist and the canopy increases its speed and descends faster.
Due to the increased cornering speed, the canopy generates more lift and climbs.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem:
What are the flight mechanics of a spiral?
1) The centrifugal force pulls the parachutists weight outwards (carousel effect).
2) The canopy is pulled by its lines into an inclined position.
3) Due to the increasing sink speed the canopy may stall.
4) Because lift acts transversely to gravity, the descent speed increases drastically in a strong rotation.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What happens to RAM-air canopies during abrupt or alternating control inputs?

options.text: I pump up the canopy and increase its flight performance.
Flight mechanically, the canopy becomes an unstable wing. It could build up extreme pendulum motion until loss of control (e.g. Line twists).
The cross ports inside the canopy ensure good dynamic pressure balance. The canopy is designed for such manoeuvres.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What happens aerodynamically on the topskin of a RAM-air canopy?

options.text: The air flows over the entire topskin and creates an area of low air pressure across the curvature because of the higher airspeed.
The air particles which are in direct contact with the surface of the topskin are physically stationary.
The layer between the fully accelerated air flow and the surface of the topskin is called 'boundary layer' from which the lift is obtained.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How can you determine if a canopy type fits to your flying experience?

options.text: Experience does not really matter, since all canopies are the same.
I only need to pay attention to the canopy size of elliptical canopies.
I can determine a suitable canopy type and size for my experience level using wing load information.
There is no size restriction for zero porosity canopies due to their high performance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What effect(s) does a high wing loading have?

options.text: The canopy flies and sinks faster in gliding flight, the flight characteristics are generally more aggressive. Incorrect control inputs have an unforgivable effect.
It is suitable for beginners to train reaction speed.
A high wing load is always used to achieve better landings in stormy winds.
There is no such thing as a too high a wing loading because the canopy stabilizes aerodynamically and thus generates the same lift with the same flight speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: The highest lift is generated on the topskin of the RAM-air canopy (approx. 2/3 from the low pressure). Which statement regarding the air flow is correct?

options.text: The air flow at the topskin is exactly the same for all canopies and is therefore unimportant.

The air impermeability of zero porosity material makes it unsuitable for topskin construction due to air congestion. This is why hybrid canopies with zero porosity material bottomskins and F-111 material topskins were developed.
The smooth surface of zero porosity material is worse for the air flowing over the topskin than F-111 fabric.

The air turbulence across F-111 fabric on the topskin interferes with the laminar air flow and thus with the lift generation. Therefore, an F-111 canopy has worse flight performance than an equally loaded zero porosity fabric canopy.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: If a canopy is flown at full speed downwind, it has a large range over ground. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It has a large glide angle.
It has a small glide angle.
It has a large angle of attack.
It has a small glide ratio.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: A parachutist flies upwind on a canopy. If he now turns 180 degrees and flies with a tailwind from now on, then

options.text: the airflow on the canopy separates.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What is the name of the point where the airflow detaches completely from the top of the wing?

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem:
Which RAM-air canopy produces more flight performance with equal size due to more lift?
1) Canopies with high aspect ratio compared to lower aspect ratio.
2) Elliptical or canopies with a bevelled rear edge compared to rectangular canopies.
3) Zero porosity material canopies compared to F-111 canopies.
4) High speed profiles compared to low speed profiles.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How do you ensure that your canopy glides further when flying with tail wind?

options.text: Search for thermals and use updrafts.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: If the headwind is so strong that the canopy does not fly forward at full speed, then there is no opportunity to gain additional propulsive power. Is this statement true?

options.text: No, because by pulling parallel on the front risers you still gain minimal propulsion, but also sink faster.
You can increase the airspeed and therefore the propulsion through a 360° rotation.
This statement is only true if I am flying with a slow flight profile canopy.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What should a parachutist expect if he flies a RAM-air canopy from a stationary air mass to a sinking one (downwash)?

options.text: an improvement in the glide angle.
an increase in the forward speed.
increased rate of descent and turbulence.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Shortly before landing, i.e. near the ground, the wind changes due to additional influences. There are changes in direction and strength due to ground friction as well as up and down winds due to thermal influences and ground shape. Therefore, your canopy will tend to want to turn out of its landing direction when it is flown into wind. What should you pay special attention to during the final approach?

options.text: Nothing, since this fact only matters for high performance canopies.
While landing the cells need to be flared asymmetrically.
When deploying, the body must be positioned against the wind in free fall to prevent an off-heading opening.
The canopy must be held in position, facing the direction of the final approach, as it does not stay on the wind axis on its own when its flown into wind.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What happens if you fly closely behind another canopy on the same flight path?

options.text: The wake could disturb my aerodynamics and it could cause problems with my canopy stability.
Because of the turbulences even more air is pumped under my canopy and this increases my lift.
I try to fly in the slipstream and increase my propulsion. This manoeuvre is especially useful for a better flare shortly before landing.
A small distance only matters if canopies don't land in the same direction and their flight paths intersect on landing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What flight behaviour does a high-speed flight profile show during a normal landing with 3-5 m/s wind?

options.text: The canopy maintains its speed and touches down.
The canopy remains at its glide angle, but the airspeed is decelerated by the flare.
The canopy merges into a flatter trajectory and planes out parallel to the ground during the flare.
The canopy glides out and sets the parachutist down on the ground when reaching its stall.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What flight behaviour does a slow-speed flight profile show during a normal landing with 3-5 m/s wind?

options.text: The canopy maintains its speed and touches down.
The canopy retains its glide angle, but the airspeed is decelerated by the flare.
The canopy merges into a flatter trajectory and planes out parallel to the ground during the flare.
The canopy glides out and sets the parachutist down on the ground when it reaches a stall.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Why shouldn't a canopy be braked abruptly to land?

options.text: Abrupt braking will swing the parachutist very far forward.
In addition to braking it will increase the angle of attack of the canopy by swinging the parachutist strongly forward.
The canopy could be dynamically stalled although it is not fully braked.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which flight behaviour and effect does a RAM-air canopy show when it is overbaked to land (stall)?

options.text: The stall may induce a fall backwards hitting the ground, injuring the parachutist badly.
A stall with its consequences is basically the goal of every landing flare.
Over-braking for landing is impossible due to the proximity of the ground and the associated ground effect. There is therefore no impact.
The overbraking ends in a absolute flare, which causes the canopy to climb again in relation to the ground (as with the pros in swoop).

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How do you fly a controlled turn with a square parachute?

options.text: Pulling down a steering line to the stop on one side.
Pull parallel on both steering lines from full speed, then quickly let the opposite steering line up again.
Look in the direction of the turn, lean your body in that direction and pull the steering line down smoothly and firmly.
The speed of the turn depends on the speed at which the steering line is pulled, not how far. Therefore, pulling the steering line quickly will result in a fast turn.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem:
What is the flight behaviour of RAM-air canopies during fast turns?
1) They lose a lot of height relative to the ground.
2) They are ideally suited to increase the airspeed before landing.
3) The turn is very steep.
4) When a fast turn is initiated, the canopy dives downwards in its flight path.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which of the canopies below has the fastest descent in a turn?

options.text: A relatively large F-111 fabric canopy.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Why are hook turns more dangerous than normal landings when landing?

options.text: The turn dynamics result in a trajectory in relation to the ground that can only be controlled with a great deal of experience and feeling.
This extreme flight manoeuvre can lead to serious landing accidents.
The flight and descent rates increase to such an extent that there is no scope for adjustments in case of false assessment.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What do I have to consider when doing a hook turn?

options.text: Hook turns may only be flown after obtaining one's licence.
A hook turn can only be flown with a fast canopy.
Every parachutist should be capable of doing a hook turn, to make the sport look impressive to spectators.
I lose a lot of height during a hook turn and therefore could easily misjudge the situation which can lead to serious injuries or death.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What is indirect steering with RAM-air canopies?

options.text: When a turn is flown from a braked condition by raising the opposite steering line.
If you get instructions how to control the canopy by radio.
When you choose the flight direction in such a way that the natural drift is directed in the desired direction.
When one parachutist steers the canopy of another parachutist while doing canopy relative work.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem:
What is meant by sashaying when flying with RAM-air canopies and how are these executed?
1) Flying a flight path that describes a figure 8 relative to the ground.
2) A flight manoeuvre where the parachutist always returns to the same position above ground and which is generally used for altitude reduction.
3) When the final approach on headwind is to high, this flight manoeuvre is used to land closer to the landing area.
4) Sashays shall be carried out in the final approach to keep the landing target in sight. They should be flown gently and controlled so that there is no danger of a collision with other parachutists.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: When can indirect steering be used with a canopy?

options.text: In the braked final approach to hold the canopy in direction.
For turning near the ground, if the loss of altitude is safe and acceptable.
For sashaying in order to reduce altitude if the final approach is set too high.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How do you generally fly slow turns with a canopy?

options.text: By small control inputs in the relevant direction.
With the front risers and the steering lines released.
Loosen the opposite leg strap during flight in order to fly the canopy into a gentle curve through shifting weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: How do you fly flat turns with a RAM-air canopy with only a little loss of altitude?

options.text: The canopy is braked (approx. 50-75%) in order to fly the desired rotation indirectly by gently raising the opposite steering line after braking.
Rotations with little loss of altitude are not sensible, because the dynamic pressure decreases so much that the canopy collapses.
For turns with little loss of altitude you need a slow flight profile.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which wind direction has the longest range and is most flexible for flying a RAM-air parachute in relation to the landing point?

options.text: The wind axis cannot be taken into account for the canopy flight as it cannot be seen.
The wind axis which will allow you to fly your planned landing pattern consisting of a crosswind base leg and final turn into wind.
Always position yourself on the wind axis so that the landing point is in front of you during the entire canopy flight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What should be considered under canopy with a crosswind?

options.text: The crosswind has no influence on the canopy flight.
Lateral drift requires constant counter-steering in order to retain direction of flight.
The rear riser must be used to hold against the wind.
The cross wind has no influence when braking.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: What needs to be considered with strong crosswind on the way to the landing area?

options.text: The cross wind can be so strong that I cannot reach my landing area.
The flaring the steering lines asymmetrically takes getting used to.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: If the steering lines are broken, a RAM-air canopy can also be steered with the rear risers. What needs to be considered?

options.text: You can quickly stall a canopy when braking.
The risers do not need to be pulled as far as brake line do to initiate a turn or to flare because of the bigger change in canopy shape.
The flight behaviour is very abrupt, for landing with the risers it is therefore advisable to do a parachute landing fall (PLF) for your own safety.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement is correct when flying turns with the risers?

options.text: The quickest turn is achieved with the front risers.
The tightest turn is achieved by the rear risers.
The most extreme turn is achieved by the opposite interaction between the rear risers and the front risers.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem:
What is the effect of steering or braking with the risers?
1) the angle of incidence specified by the manufacturer is changed.
2) the trim during the steering manoeuvre is changed. Not all canopy types will remain stable in flight.
3) there is a risk of one-sided overloading of the individual cells because only the weight bearing cell walls are affected
4) You change the shape of the canopy from that intended by the manufacturer. This can have a very aggressive effect on the flight behaviour.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement is correct in relation to RAM-air canopies?

options.text: Gravity is the predominant force acting on the canopy, acting on the mass of the parachutist.
The weight is transferred to the canopy by the angle of attack. Thereby the canopy starts to glide.
By gliding, the canopy creates the airflow that produces dynamic pressure. The value of the dynamic pressure must always be higher than the weight of the parachutist.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement regarding the opening behaviour of canopies is correct?

options.text: The opening shock is a little harder without a slider, but also faster. This fact is useful for reserve canopies leading to their very short opening distance.
It takes time and therefore altitude to fill canopies with sufficient air as they open.
The deployment distance of a canopy is always the same regardless of how it is packed.
The minimum deployment height of a main canopy above ground is calculated by adding the deployment distances of the main and reserve canopies.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement is correct with regard to flying canopies?

options.text: I can always learn new steering tactics. Defensive and foresighted flying is the safest flying style.
In turbulent conditions, a canopy in full flight is most stable.
In air traffic, I have to be constantly aware of my position, where I want to go and where others are.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement is correct regarding landing?

options.text: Everyone always lands in the same direction. That's why it's completely safe for many people to land parallel, side by side and close together
Obstacles and danger areas must not deter me from my final approach direction.
Many parachutists land simultaneously in the landing area. Therefore, the air traffic there is often very dense and dangerous if not navigated with care.
You don't have to pay attention to landing parachutist after your own landing, because they have a better view from the air anyway and will avoid you.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement regarding planning of the landing approach is correct?

options.text: It is better to turn to a suitable alternate landing area at an early stage than to get into difficulties by continuing the planned landing approach (e.g. due to obstacles, low turns at the last moment, canopy collision, etc.).
Despite air traffic, I correct my final approach to my pre-planned direction, since priority in the air is given on the principle of completed manoeuvres.
I always try to be the lowest canopy, because then I have the whole airspace for myself and don't need to get in order.
I always try to reach the landing area by all possible means (e.g. hook-turn, cutting away or ignoring wind), because otherwise I attract negative attention and am criticized.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics
questions.stem: Which statement is correct for the open, airworthy canopy?

options.text: A canopy should fly normally after its full opening. I can determine whether this is the case visually and with a control and brake checks.
A canopy will not change its shape without my intervention (turning, stalling or collapsing). If it does, I have either a nuisance factor or malfunction
imprudent steering can endanger me and others significantly.

questions.stem: Do I have to pay attention to the seams on my harness? 1) A regular visual inspection should be routine. 2) In case of damage I should ask for competent advice (e.g. Rigger or Fallschirmwart). 3) I have to maintain small seams myself. 4) No, because a routine inspection every 10 months regulates this.
